title: Moving file uploads
question: Should we move customer file uploads to a new storage provider, change how uploads reach storage, or both?
summary: A mid-size web team stores customers' files with one storage provider. Large uploads time out, and the transfer bill keeps growing. This map shows how an upload works today, what each option changes, and what the team still has to decide. All figures are made up.

checked.note: Checked against the incident review, a provider comparison and a team discussion.

glossary.signed link: A web address that lets one browser upload or download one file for a few minutes, without a password.
glossary.proxy: When our servers pass every byte between the customer and storage, instead of the customer talking to storage directly.
glossary.resumable upload: An upload sent in pieces, so a dropped connection only loses the last piece.
glossary.data out: Files sent from storage to anyone outside it. Providers charge for this.

evidence.text: Uploads over 200 MB timed out for about 40 minutes.
Half our servers were just shovelling bytes. Nothing else could get through.
Our storage bill grew 22% last quarter, mostly from data transfer out, not storage.
Support received 31 tickets. Most from customers uploading video.
Data out: $90 per TB today; $0 to our CDN with provider B.
Moving 180 TB at current transfer prices would cost about $16,000 once. Provider B offers free one-time transfer over 100 TB, on request.
The real problem is the proxy, not the provider. Direct uploads fix the timeouts wherever the files live.
Customers ask for a progress bar and the ability to resume after a dropped connection.
Signed links must expire in minutes and only allow one file path.
Nobody has tested how virus scanning works if files no longer pass through our servers.

maps.title: How an upload works
maps.intro: Each journey is a numbered path. Each column is the part of the system that does that step.

journeys.title: Upload today
journeys.summary: Every byte passes through our servers on its way to storage.

steps.text: Customer picks a file and presses Upload
Browser sends the whole file to our servers
steps.pain: No progress bar; a dropped connection starts again.

steps.text: Our servers pass the bytes on to storage
steps.detail: Streaming proxy in the upload service; 60-second idle timeout at the load balancer.

steps.text: A job scans the file for viruses
steps.detail: Scanner reads the file from storage after the upload finishes.

steps.text: File is marked ready and shown to the customer

journeys.title: Upload with direct links (proposed)
journeys.summary: The browser sends the file straight to storage using a short-lived signed link.

steps.text: Customer picks a file and presses Upload
Our servers check the customer may upload, and issue a signed link for one file
Browser uploads straight to storage in pieces, with a progress bar
Storage tells us the upload finished; a job scans it
File is marked ready only after a clean scan

maps.title: Options
maps.intro: The outcome at the top, then the problems that stand in its way, the ideas for each, and the quick tests that would prove an idea.

root.title: Big uploads always finish, and the transfer bill falls

children.title: Ship to 5% of video uploads for two weeks
children.text: Compare failure rate and server load.

children.title: Raise the idle timeout to 10 minutes on one server
Copy one month of new files to B and serve them through the CDN
children.text: Measure the bill and download speed.

children.title: Cache popular downloads at the CDN
Turn on caching for public files only
children.text: One week, then compare data out.

gaps.title: Direct uploads with a progress bar and resume
gaps.why: Fixes the timeouts no matter which provider we use.

stories.as: As a customer uploading a large video on a weak connection, I want the upload to resume where it stopped, so I do not start again.
done_when: a 2 GB upload survives a 30-second disconnect
the progress bar matches the bytes received
our servers handle no file bytes

gaps.title: Scan files that never touch our servers
gaps.why: Today scanning assumes we saw the upload.

stories.as: As the security engineer, I want every upload scanned before anyone can download it, so direct uploads add no risk.
done_when: a file is not downloadable until its scan passes
an infected test file is quarantined and the customer is told

gaps.title: Move existing files to provider B
gaps.why: Cuts the data-out bill; only worth it if the free transfer is granted.

stories.as: As finance, I want the move to cost nothing up front, so the saving shows before the September review.
done_when: provider B confirms free transfer in writing
every file's checksum matches after the copy
downloads switch over with no broken links

notes.title: The proxy is the bottleneck
notes.body: Servers hold a connection for the whole upload. That is why everything slowed down.
notes.recommend: Do direct uploads first; it is independent of the provider choice.
notes.question: Do we agree to separate the two decisions: direct uploads now, provider later?

notes.title: Signed links must be narrow
notes.body: A link that allows any path, or lasts hours, would let anyone write files into our storage.
notes.recommend: Links last 10 minutes, cover one path, and set a size limit.
notes.question: Is 10 minutes long enough for the slowest customers, given uploads resume in pieces?

notes.title: Nothing is downloadable before it is scanned
notes.body: With direct uploads, a file lands in storage before we have looked at it.
notes.recommend: Upload into a holding area; move it to the live area only after a clean scan.
notes.question: Who builds and tests the holding area before the 5% trial?

notes.title: Customers asked for two things
notes.body: A progress bar and resuming after a dropped connection. Neither needs a new provider.
notes.recommend: Ship both with direct uploads, and tell the 31 customers who raised tickets.
notes.question: Do we contact the customers who reported the problem when the fix ships?

notes.title: The bill problem is data out, not storage
notes.body: Storage grew a little; data out grew a lot.
notes.recommend: Try CDN caching first; it is cheap and fast to test.
notes.question: How much must data out fall by September for this to count as fixed?

notes.title: Only move if the transfer is free
notes.body: At $16,000, the move pays back in about seven months. Free transfer makes it pay back at once.
notes.recommend: Ask provider B for free transfer in writing before deciding.
notes.question: Who asks provider B, and by when?

notes.title: Two outcomes, two clocks
notes.body: Timeouts hurt customers now. The bill matters by September.
notes.recommend: Fix timeouts this month; decide the provider in July with test results in hand.
notes.question: Is July the right month to make the provider decision?

notes.title: Say what the trial must show
notes.body: Without a target, a two-week trial cannot pass or fail.
notes.recommend: Pass if failed uploads drop below 1% and no server spends more than 5% of its time on uploads.
notes.question: Are those the right pass marks for the trial?

notes.title: Tell people what is happening
notes.body: Today a big upload shows a spinner with no end.
notes.recommend: Show bytes sent, time left, and a clear message if the connection drops.
notes.question: Should a dropped upload resume by itself, or ask first?

notes.title: An assistant can check the copy
notes.body: Comparing checksums for millions of files is repetitive and easy to get wrong by hand.
notes.recommend: Let an agent run and report the checksum comparison; a person signs off the switch-over.
notes.question: Who signs off the switch-over once the agent's report is clean?

notes.title: Nobody has run provider B
notes.body: Four years of experience with the current provider; none with B.
notes.recommend: Run the one-month copy test before committing.
notes.question: Are we willing to run two providers for a few months during the move?

decisions.question: Do we build direct uploads now, separately from the provider choice?
decisions.decision: Yes. Direct uploads ship to 5% of video uploads in June.
